title: India Is Sticking With America—for Now
gist: An Indian scholar argues that despite Trump's tariffs, secondary-sanctions threats, and tilt toward Pakistan and China, India has not ruptured with Washington but pursues an 'America plus' strategy—deepening ties with the U.S. and its allies while hedging with Russia and China—because no alternative patron can match U.S. markets, capital, and technology; but proposed 100% tariffs on Russian-oil buyers and eroding domestic support for Modi could force his hand.

insights.claim: India has adopted an 'America plus' strategy—sustaining partnership with the United States while widening engagement with other powers, mainly U.S. allies—rather than the rupture or multialignment some predicted.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: Clarifies that India's hedging still centers on the U.S., anchoring the base case for U.S.-India defense, trade, and tech ties.
insights.quote: New Delhi has adopted what might be called an “America plus” strategy
insights.locator: Yet these strains have not led to the rupture

insights.claim: When India has diversified, it has done so mostly with U.S. allies—Australia, Canada, Japan, the UK, and European countries—signing free trade agreements with New Zealand, the UK, and the EU rather than pivoting to China's blocs.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: India's diversification reinforces rather than replaces the Western orbit—relevant to supply-chain and trade realignment bets.
insights.locator: Many analysts argue that these overtures

insights.claim: Modi has responded to Trump's provocations with unusual restraint, resisting demands to pull away from Washington while continuing trade talks, deepening defense cooperation, and preserving the Quad.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: Modi's restraint is the load-bearing variable holding the relationship together—its limits define the tail risk.
insights.locator: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has responded

insights.claim: Trump has tested the relationship by slapping tariffs on India, threatening secondary sanctions, getting closer to Pakistan, and engaging China—the country India considers its biggest long-term military threat.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: Catalogs the specific frictions that could still tip India away from Washington—each is a monitorable escalation vector.
insights.locator: President Donald Trump, in his second term

insights.claim: By late 2025 India faced some of the highest tariffs of any U.S. partner, punished for protectionism and for buying Russian oil, even though Washington had carved exceptions for itself and European countries.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: The perceived double standard on Russian oil is the specific grievance most likely to reawaken Indian anti-Americanism.

insights.claim: Trump elevated Pakistan by taking credit for ending the May 2025 India-Pakistan conflict, favoring army chief Syed Asim Munir, and using Islamabad as a mediator with Iran—moves India rejected as violating its bilateral-only stance.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: U.S. re-warming to Pakistan directly undercuts a core Indian red line—a structural irritant in the relationship.

insights.claim: Trump has spent significant time engaging Xi Jinping, talked loosely of a 'G-2,' and failed to hold annual Quad summits, raising doubts about U.S. commitment to balancing China across Asia.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: A U.S.-China 'G-2' drift would strand India's China-balancing bet—key uncertainty for Indo-Pacific security positioning.
insights.locator: Trump also became friendlier with China

themes.theme: Why India has no better patron

insights.claim: India has no better great-power patron because China and Russia will never buy Indian goods and services on the U.S. scale, nor can Russia help India balance China.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: The structural absence of alternatives is why the relationship survives friction—the durable floor under U.S.-India ties.
insights.quote: when it comes to cultivating a great-power patron, India doesn’t have better options
insights.locator: After all, when it comes to cultivating

insights.claim: U.S.-India goods and services trade reached $240 billion in 2025 with a surplus in India's favor, while India ran a goods deficit of well over $110 billion with China in the same year.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: The trade math—U.S. surplus for India vs. a lopsided China deficit—quantifies why Washington remains India's indispensable market.
insights.quote: U.S.-Indian trade, in goods and services, reached $240 billion in 2025, with a surplus in India’s favor.
insights.locator: India recognizes that neither China nor Russia

insights.claim: The U.S. and India finalized a consequential trade deal in February 2026 promising to raise bilateral trade to $500 billion by 2030, but Trump has yet to sign off and keeps seeking new ways to impose tariffs.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: The unsigned $500B trade deal is a concrete catalyst—its ratification or collapse is a binary event for the relationship.

insights.claim: China spends four times more on defense than India, has a massive military presence in Tibet, expanding Indian Ocean naval reach, and deepening ties with Pakistan, leaving the conventional border balance favoring Beijing.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: The 4:1 defense-spending gap is why India can't credibly turn to China and needs U.S. security access—the strategic logic of alignment.
insights.locator: India also relies on the United States

insights.claim: Russia, since its 2022 invasion of Ukraine, is too reliant on China to meaningfully balance Beijing, so India cannot use Moscow, BRICS, or the Shanghai Cooperation Organization as a China-balancing counterweight.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: Removes the Russia-hedge option from India's toolkit, further locking in its dependence on the U.S. for balancing China.
insights.locator: India couldn’t turn to China or Russia

insights.claim: The U.S.-India relationship has acquired a resilience that neither Trump's volatility nor India's anti-American tendencies can easily undo, with India's economic ambitions, military planning, and tech aspirations now revolving around the United States.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: Argues the partnership is structurally embedded, not personality-dependent—supporting a base case of continuity through turbulence.
insights.quote: the U.S.-Indian relationship has acquired a resilience that neither Trump’s volatility nor India’s long-standing anti-American tendencies can easily undo
insights.locator: By the time Trump returned to office

insights.claim: India finalized a new ten-year defense framework with the U.S. last year and preserved the Quad by hosting a foreign-ministers meeting when Trump refused to attend the leaders' summit.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence India is actively investing to keep the security architecture alive despite U.S. wavering.
insights.locator: Modi has mostly ignored these calls

insights.claim: The most immediate danger is proposed U.S. legislation authorizing tariffs of up to 100 percent on countries buying Russian energy; if it passes without an India waiver it would damage India's economy and reawaken dormant anti-Americanism.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: The 100% Russian-energy tariff bill is the single highest-probability trigger for a real rupture—a specific legislative event to track.
insights.quote: proposed U.S. legislation that would authorize tariffs of up to 100 percent on countries that buy Russian energy

insights.claim: Recent youth protests over leaked exam papers have pierced Modi's aura of invulnerability, and eroding domestic authority could push him to find defying Washington politically useful.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: Modi's domestic weakness is the transmission channel by which anti-American sentiment could translate into policy—watch his political standing.
insights.locator: Until recently, Modi’s domestic political dominance

insights.claim: A rupture wouldn't necessarily be formal but could slow defense and tech cooperation, push India toward Chinese investment and away from U.S. weapons, and end India's moderating role in diluting BRICS efforts to dethrone the U.S. dollar.
insights.speaker: C. Raja Mohan
insights.so_what: Names the downstream consequences—including India ceasing to blunt de-dollarization efforts—that a breakdown would unleash.
